title: Local Ancestry and Model Complexity
subtitle: When the extra parameters only cost power
learningObjectives: Recognize local-ancestry terms as parameters, and parameters as a cost that falls hardest on small samples.
Predict when a local-ancestry model adds nothing: similar effects and similar frequencies across backgrounds.
Explain why the same modelling choice is free in a large cohort and decisive in a small one.

prediction.question: At this locus the effect is the same on every ancestry background and the allele frequencies are similar. In an admixed study of 500 people adjusted for age, sex and ten global PCs, which of global ancestry PCs alone, adding a local-ancestry covariate, and the local-ancestry interaction model detect it at p < 0.05?

options.label: Global PCs and the local-ancestry covariate, but not the interaction model

interpretation.prompt: The effect is the same on every ancestry background. Does modelling local ancestry help, hurt, or neither?
interpretation.whatChanged: Every model estimates the same effect; only the uncertainty differs, and it differs by what each added term explains. Global PCs and the local-ancestry covariate are within a hair of each other, because the allele frequencies barely differ by background, so local ancestry explains about 0.5% of the genotype variance: nothing to correct, almost nothing to pay. The interaction model fits one slope per background and tests them jointly on three degrees of freedom, so it first detects the locus near n=900 where the single-slope models cross near n=450. The covariate switches show the other two cases: three clinical covariates take the global-PC p-value from 0.031 to 0.016 at n=500, because they explain a fifth of LDL variance; sixty technical indicators move it to 0.041, and at n=250 from 0.131 to 0.187, because they explain almost nothing and cost sixty terms.
interpretation.whyItMatters: A term earns its place by what it explains. Clinical covariates explain the outcome and buy power; technical indicators explain little and cost k/n; local ancestry explains genotype variance, which is a cost unless the backgrounds differ; and an interaction model pays in degrees of freedom. Local ancestry can fail, not because the model is wrong but because complexity was added that the locus did not need, and every one of these prices falls hardest where the sample is smallest, which is exactly the admixed and underrepresented cohorts the method was built for. Module 3 shows when the extra parameters pay for themselves; this module shows what they cost when they do not.
interpretation.facilitatorNote: Introduce from module 3: the same three models and the same admixed composition, but a locus where the backgrounds agree and the allele frequencies are similar (APOE rs7412: 0.11 / 0.08 / 0.06). Park the slider at 500: global PCs and the covariate model are significant with near-identical intervals, the interaction model is not, and every point estimate is the same. That is the module in one screen. The near-identical first two arms are deliberate and worth saying: a local-ancestry covariate is cheap and, here, useless; the interaction model is neither. Then the two switches: clinical covariates make every model more significant (they explain LDL), sixty technical indicators make every model less significant, most at n=250. Slide to 1,200 and all three models agree, which is why the same choice is free in a biobank and decisive in a small study. Then put the two modules together: there is no one right way, and the answer depends on whether the effect differs between backgrounds and on what each covariate actually explains, which you cannot know before you look.

alleleFrequencies.note: APOE epsilon-2 defining variant. Frequencies are broadly similar across continental groups, so ancestry adjustment removes little confounding here while still consuming degrees of freedom.

realInputs.ancestryDistribution: All of Us Research Program, genomic data release v7 (~245,000 short-read whole genomes); ancestry proportions rounded to whole percent.

syntheticInputs: The shared effect size (0.24 phenotype SD per allele on every background) is chosen for legibility; it is not a published APOE effect estimate.
The local-ancestry composition is fixed at module 3's default (50% African, with the remainder in a 0.31:0.17 European-to-Admixed American ratio), and the sample-size slider is the admixed study's n.

Covariate blocks: clinical (BMI, smoking, statin use; 3 terms explaining 20% of LDL variance) and technical (genotyping batch, site, plate; 60 indicators explaining 2%). The term counts and explained variances are illustrative of a biobank LDL analysis, not drawn from a specific study; explained variances add.
assumptions: Additive dosage model, Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, continuous phenotype standardised to unit variance.
Global-PC model: slope = sum(p_g f_g b_g) / sum(p_g f_g), the marginal regression. Global principal components carry no locus-specific ancestry information, so they leave this slope unchanged.

Local-ancestry-covariate model: slope = sum(p_g f_g (1-f_g) b_g) / sum(p_g f_g (1-f_g)), the within-background slope weighted by genotype variance; its standard error subtracts the genotype variance that ancestry explains.

Local-ancestry-interaction model: one slope per background, with standard errors from the background's sample size and allele frequency, tested jointly on three degrees of freedom. This is the local-ancestry-deconvolved (Tractor-style) regression, reduced to a single locus.
Covariate counts: 12 (age, sex, ten PCs), 13 (plus local-ancestry dosage), and 16 (plus per-background genotype terms); each absorbs k/n of the genotype variance by chance.
Power for the interaction model is that of the three-degree-of-freedom joint test (non-central chi-squared); for the single-slope models it is the two-sided Wald test.

A covariate block costs k/n of the genotype variance by chance and shrinks the residual by the outcome variance it explains; the interaction model's per-background slopes pay the block's chance share against the whole cohort, since the covariates are fit once.
provenance.derived: Standard errors, p-values, power, meta-analysis summaries, and heterogeneity statistics are computed from the inputs above by analysis/genetics.py; none are hand-entered.
